questions.q: Which description of the event loop is right?
questions.explain: After each task, the microtask queue is drained completely, including microtasks added during the drain. Only then does the next task start.
options: Run one microtask, then one task, alternating
Run one task to completion, then every microtask until the queue is empty, then the next task
Run all tasks, then all microtasks
Run whichever callback was scheduled first, task or microtask

questions.q: A request handler runs a synchronous loop for 300 ms. A timer was due after 10 ms. When does the timer's callback run?
questions.explain: Run to completion: nothing interrupts a running task. The due timer waits in the task queue until the stack is empty and microtasks are drained.
options: After 10 ms, pausing the loop
In parallel with the loop, on another thread
After the loop and the rest of the handler finish, and after any microtasks
Never; timers that are late are dropped

questions.q: Where do the timer and network features that feed the task queue come from?
questions.explain: The language defines promises and the microtask queue (called jobs in the specification). Timers, I/O and events are provided by the host, which queues their callbacks as tasks.
options: The ECMAScript language itself
The host: the browser or Node.js, which embeds the JavaScript engine
The V8 garbage collector
The operating system calls JavaScript functions directly

questions.q: Which of these is scheduled as a microtask?
questions.explain: Code after await, promise handlers and queueMicrotask callbacks are microtasks. Timers, events, I/O and setImmediate are tasks.
options: A setTimeout(fn, 0) callback
A click handler
The rest of an async function after await
A setImmediate callback

questions.q: A cart's add method may be called ten times in one task. What does scheduling the "save cart" call with queueMicrotask (once per task) achieve?
questions.explain: Batching: the first change schedules one microtask; later changes in the same task just add to the pending state. The flush still happens before anything else in the task queue.
options: The cart is saved ten times, but faster
All ten changes are saved once, right after the current task, before any timer or I/O runs
The save is delayed until the next timer
The save runs on another thread

questions.q: How does queueMicrotask(fn) differ from Promise.resolve().then(fn)?
questions.explain: Same queue, same timing. queueMicrotask states the intent directly and does not turn errors into promise rejections.
options: queueMicrotask runs fn as a task, after timers
queueMicrotask runs fn synchronously
Both put fn in the microtask queue; queueMicrotask creates no promise, and a throw in fn is reported as an uncaught exception instead of a rejected promise
There is no difference at all

questions.q: In Node.js, when do process.nextTick callbacks run?
questions.explain: Node keeps a separate nextTick queue, drained after each callback just before the promise microtask queue. (The one exception is the top-level code of an ES module, which Node runs from its promise-based module loader: there, promise microtasks queued by that code run first.)
options: In the check phase, with setImmediate
In the timers phase
As soon as the current callback finishes, before the promise microtasks
Only when the process is about to exit

questions.q: In Node.js, a long job runs in pieces and wants to let pending I/O (incoming requests) be handled between pieces. Which should schedule the next piece?
questions.explain: setImmediate runs in the check phase, after the poll phase has handled I/O. nextTick and microtasks run before the loop moves on, so they would starve I/O.
options: process.nextTick
queueMicrotask
setImmediate
Promise.resolve().then

questions.q: A function reschedules itself forever with process.nextTick. What happens to a server's incoming requests?
questions.explain: The nextTick queue (like the microtask queue) is drained completely before the loop moves on. An endless chain starves everything else.
options: They are handled between ticks as usual
They are never handled: the nextTick queue never empties, so the loop never reaches the poll phase
Node throws a RangeError after 1,000 ticks
They are handled on a second thread

questions.q: Which of these exists only in Node.js, not in browsers?
questions.explain: setImmediate and process.nextTick are Node APIs. Portable code uses queueMicrotask and setTimeout.
options: queueMicrotask
setTimeout
setImmediate and process.nextTick
Promise.resolve

questions.q: A loop does await null on every iteration for 2 seconds. Can a 0 ms timer that was queued before the loop run during those 2 seconds?
questions.explain: Awaiting an already-available value resumes in the same microtask drain. To let tasks run, you must return to the task queue, for example by awaiting a timer.
options: Yes, every await gives the timer a turn
No: each await only goes through the microtask queue, which is drained before any task, so the timer waits
Yes, but only every 1,000 iterations
No, because await null throws

questions.q: Why does the export use a time budget per slice (process rows until about 8 ms have passed) rather than a fixed number of rows?
questions.explain: What matters to other work is how long each slice holds the thread. A time budget bounds that directly; a row count only bounds it on the machine you tested.
options: Fixed counts are not allowed in async functions
Rows differ in cost and machines differ in speed; a time budget keeps each slice short everywhere
It makes the total export faster than the blocking version
setTimeout requires a time budget

questions.q: Compared with doing it in one go, a time-sliced export…
questions.explain: Slicing does the same work, plus a little overhead for each yield. It does not make the work parallel; it shares the thread fairly. Truly heavy work belongs in a worker thread or a job queue.
options: finishes much sooner
takes slightly longer in total, but other work (requests, health checks) keeps running during it
runs on several CPU cores
uses no main-thread time

questions.q: A report takes 20 seconds of pure computation. What is the best way to keep the server responsive?
questions.explain: Slicing 20 seconds of work only spreads the slowdown. A worker thread has its own event loop and runs in parallel, so the main loop stays free for requests.
options: Add more await statements inside the loop
Wrap the loop in Promise.all
Run it in a worker thread or a background job, off the main thread
Use process.nextTick between rows

questions.q: What does event-loop lag measure?
questions.explain: A healthy loop runs timers within a millisecond or two of their due time. Large lag means long tasks (or microtask chains) are blocking the thread, so every request waits.
options: How long a network request takes
How many callbacks are in the task queue
How late timers run compared with when they were due, which shows how long tasks are holding the thread
The time the garbage collector takes

questions.q: In a browser, a microtask chain runs for 3 seconds. What happens to the page?
questions.explain: The render step comes after the microtask drain. A long microtask chain blocks rendering and input exactly like a long synchronous task.
options: It keeps repainting between microtasks
It freezes: rendering happens between tasks, after the microtask queue is empty
The browser moves the microtasks to a worker
Only clicks are delayed; painting continues

questions.q: A retry helper waits 30 seconds between attempts. How do you test it without the test taking minutes?
questions.explain: Fake timers replace setTimeout with a clock the test controls, so a 30-second wait is tested instantly and deterministically.
options: Lower the wait to 30 ms only in production
Use fake timers (for example vi.useFakeTimers()) and move the clock forward in the test
Skip the test
Replace setTimeout with queueMicrotask

questions.q: Code works only because one promise chain happens to finish two microtask steps before another. What is the right fix?
questions.explain: Step counts change when anyone refactors (one more await, one fewer then). If B needs A, express the dependency; do not rely on accidental timing.
options: Add an extra .then(() => {}) to be safe
Make the second piece of work explicitly wait for the first (await it or chain on it)
Use setTimeout(…, 0) to push it later
Nothing, microtask step counts never change

questions.q: Finish reportLow(sku) so that all SKUs reported during one task are printed in a single line ALERT: A, B, C, without duplicates, using queueMicrotask.
questions.explain: The first report in a task schedules one flush; later reports only add to the set, which removes duplicates. The report in the later timer task starts a new batch.

questions.q: The loop sends 20 reminders, but the timer queued before it cannot run until all are sent. Add a yieldToLoop helper that awaits a 0 ms timer, and call it after each reminder so the timer runs after the first one.
questions.explain: Awaiting a resolved promise stays in the microtask queue. Awaiting a timer puts the rest of the loop behind the waiting timer, so the timer runs right after reminder 1 (position 1 in the log).

questions.q: Finish processInSlices(items, perSlice, fn): call fn on each item, and after every perSlice items (but not after the last one) await a 0 ms timer. Return how many slices were used.
questions.explain: Seven items in slices of three gives 3 + 3 + 1. The yields between slices return to the task queue, so the interval's task gets to run.

questions.q: Add one await somewhere inside saveOrder so the program prints the lines in the order shown.
questions.explain: An async function runs synchronously until its first await. Putting the await between the two logs makes the second one a microtask that runs after responding.

questions.q: Finish monitorLag(ms): start a setInterval every ms milliseconds that records how late each tick is (actual time minus expected time), and return a stop() function that clears the interval and returns the worst lag.
questions.explain: Each tick compares when it ran with when it should have run. During the 200 ms block no tick can run, so the first tick after it is late by roughly 190 ms or more.

questions.q: Two chains take turns and print stock 1, email 1, stock 2, email 2. Change the code so the stock chain finishes completely before the email chain starts, printing the expected lines.
questions.explain: If the email steps must wait for the stock steps, say so: chain them after the stock chain (or await it). Relying on queue positions would break with the next refactor.
